name: Sugar-free gum

lead: Sugar-free gum is chewing gum sweetened with sugar alcohols such as xylitol, sorbitol or maltitol. People chew it to freshen breath for a while and keep the mouth moist.

Chewing stimulates saliva, which clears food debris and buffers plaque acids, and dental researchers describe saliva as protective for teeth. Clinical trials of sugar-free gum have focused on cavities, including gums with added calcium-phosphate complexes for enamel remineralisation. Wikipedia notes that evidence for gum as a halitosis treatment is not supported by strong data.

paras: People chew a piece after meals or before social situations, in place of mints or sugary gum. The breath effect lasts while chewing and a short time after.
Large amounts of sorbitol or mannitol can cause gas or diarrhoea. Swallowed gum is a concern for young children.

angle.text: Sugar-free gum freshens breath for a while and boosts saliva, which dental researchers describe as protective for teeth. The dental trials concern cavities rather than appearance.

lead: Sugar-free chewing gum is gum sweetened with sugar alcohols such as xylitol, sorbitol, maltitol or isomalt, often with small amounts of intense sweeteners such as aspartame or sucralose.[1] In oral-care and appearance discussions it is used mainly to freshen breath temporarily and to stimulate saliva, which dental researchers describe as protective for teeth.[2][3]

Clinical research on sugar-free gum has focused on tooth decay rather than looks. A review of clinical caries trials examined whether gum-induced salivary flow helps clear food particles and neutralise plaque acids,[4] and trials have tested gums containing added calcium-phosphate complexes for enamel remineralisation.[3][5] Wikipedia notes that evidence for gum as a halitosis treatment is not supported by strong data.[6]
infobox: Xylitol, sorbitol, maltitol, isomalt, aspartame, sucralose[1]

paras: Sugar alcohols typically make up roughly 40 to 50 percent of a sugar-free gum formula, and their cooling sensation on dissolving is part of the gum's appeal.[1] Some products add fluoride or calcium compounds intended to support enamel.[1]

Chewing gum-like substances are very old; chicle from Central America and spruce resin in North America were chewed long before commercial gum appeared in the mid-1800s, and synthetic rubber had replaced chicle by the 1960s.[1] Sugar-free versions grew out of interest in sugar substitutes and caries prevention, reviewed in the dental literature from the late 1990s.[7]

Chewing increases salivary flow. Saliva dilutes and clears food debris, buffers plaque acids and supplies minerals to enamel, and reviews in the Journal of the American Dental Association describe these as protective functions.[2][4] Studies of sugar alcohols have also examined whether xylitol and sorbitol have direct caries-preventive effects.[8]

A review of seven clinical trials assessed chewing gum's effect on caries incidence and on mechanisms such as plaque acid neutralisation.[4] Randomised, double-blind in situ trials tested sugar-free gum with casein phosphopeptide-amorphous calcium phosphate (CPP-ACP) for remineralising enamel lesions and increasing their acid resistance,[3][5] and a bitewing radiography study examined its effect on approximal caries.[9] Other work looked at whether stimulating saliva reduces enamel erosion in in situ and ex vivo models.[10] A community-level study examined caries prevention from sugar-substituted gum.[11] These studies address dental health; none of the reviewed material tests gum as a treatment for appearance.

Large amounts of sorbitol- or mannitol-containing products can cause gas or diarrhoea, and absorption patterns differ between healthy people and people with irritable bowel syndrome.[1][12] Wikipedia also lists swallowed-gum concerns in young children and ongoing research into microplastics released during chewing.[1]
Gum is mentioned in appearance communities as a low-cost way to keep breath fresh and mouth moist. Discussion of hard-chewing gum for jaw development is a separate topic covered under its own entry.

lore.intro: Sugar-free gum is treated in oral-care discussions as an easy add-on for breath and saliva.

timeline.event: Commercial spruce gum is sold in the United States.[1]
Synthetic rubber replaces chicle in gum bases.[1]
A British Dental Journal review examines sugar substitutes, gum and caries.[7]
In situ trials test CPP-ACP sugar-free gum for enamel remineralisation.[3][5]
